prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Let $DABC$ be a corner pyramid with apex $D$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, $P$ the foot of the altitude from $D$ to $\triangle ABC$, and $AB=1$. Compute $DM$.

solutions.title: Median to the hypotenuse
solutions.body:
$DA=DB=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ since $\triangle DAB$ is an isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse $AB=1$. $DM$ is the median to the hypotenuse, so $DM=\frac12AB=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

solutions.title: Centroid of the base
solutions.body:
Since $DA=DB=DC$, the foot $P$ of the altitude is the centre (centroid) of the equilateral triangle $ABC$. Then $MC=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $P$ divides $CM$ with $CP:PM=2:1$, so $MP=\frac13\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{\sqrt3}6=\frac1{2\sqrt3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}6$**

solutions.title: Right triangle DPM
solutions.body:
$\triangle DPM$ is right-angled at $P$ with $DM=\frac12$ and $MP=\frac{\sqrt3}6$: $DP^2=\frac14-\frac1{12}=\frac16$, so $DP=\frac1{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}6$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{\sqrt6}$**

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, $P$ the foot of the altitude from $D$ to $\triangle ABC$, and $AB=1$. Compute $\cos\angle DMP$.

solutions.title: Right triangle DPM
solutions.body:
In the right triangle $DPM$, $\cos\angle DMP=\frac{MP}{DM}=\frac{\sqrt3/6}{1/2}=\frac{\sqrt3}3=\frac1{\sqrt3}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{\sqrt3}$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$, $P$ its centre and $M$ the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. The cornered square is built by attaching to the square the pyramid $EABCD$ (apex $E$ above $P$, all faces equilateral triangles) and then attaching corner pyramids with apexes $F,G,H,I$ to the faces $EAB$, $EBC$, $ECD$, $EDA$ respectively (see the figure). Compute $\cos\angle FMP$.

solutions.title: Double the base angle
solutions.body:
Pyramid $EABCD$ is the union of the four corner pyramids $PABE$, $PBCE$, $PCDE$, $PDAE$ (apex $P$). Let $\theta=\angle EMP$, the base angle of such a corner pyramid; by problem 1(d), $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$. The corner pyramid with apex $F$ on face $EAB$ has the same base angle: $\angle FME=\theta$. The points $F,E,P$ lie in the plane through $M$ perpendicular to $AB$, on opposite sides of $ME$, so $\angle FMP=2\theta$ and
$$\cos\angle FMP=2\cos^2\theta-1=2\cdot\frac13-1=-\frac13.$$

**Answer: $-\frac13$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$, $P$ its centre and $M$ the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. The cornered square is built by attaching to the square the pyramid $EABCD$ (apex $E$ above $P$, all faces equilateral triangles) and then attaching corner pyramids with apexes $F,G,H,I$ to the faces $EAB$, $EBC$, $ECD$, $EDA$ respectively (see the figure). Compute the cosine of the angle formed by planes $FEB$ and $GEB$ (that is, $\cos\angle FNG$ where $N$ is the midpoint of $\overline{EB}$ and $NF\perp EB$, $NG\perp EB$).

solutions.title: Angles around the edge EB
solutions.body:
Let $N$ be the midpoint of $EB$. In the plane through $N$ perpendicular to $EB$ we see (from $F$ round to $G$) the rays $NF$, $NA$, $NP$, $NC$, $NG$: since $\triangle FEB$ is a right isosceles triangle, $NF\perp EB$, and similarly for $G$, and $NA,NC\perp EB$ as $EAB$, $EBC$ are equilateral; $NP\perp EB$ since $\triangle PEB$ is right isosceles. The angles $\angle FNA$, $\angle ANP$, $\angle PNC$, $\angle CNG$ are all base angles of corner pyramids, equal to $\theta$ (with $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$). So the reflex angle from $F$ to $G$ is $4\theta$ and $\angle FNG=2\pi-4\theta$. Then
$$\cos\angle FNG=\cos4\theta=2\cos^2 2\theta-1=2\left(-\tfrac13\right)^2-1=-\frac79.$$

**Answer: $-\frac79$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$, $P$ its centre and $M$ the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. The cornered square is built by attaching to the square the pyramid $EABCD$ (apex $E$ above $P$, all faces equilateral triangles) and then attaching corner pyramids with apexes $F,G,H,I$ to the faces $EAB$, $EBC$, $ECD$, $EDA$ respectively (see the figure). Compute the perimeter of $FGHI$.

solutions.title: Law of Cosines
solutions.body:
With $N$ the midpoint of $EB$: $FN=GN=\frac12$ (median to the hypotenuse of the right isosceles triangles $FEB$, $GEB$). By the Law of Cosines in $\triangle FNG$ with $\cos\angle FNG=-\frac79$:
$$FG^2=\frac14+\frac14-2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\left(-\frac79\right)=\frac12+\frac7{18}=\frac89,\qquad FG=\frac{2\sqrt2}3.$$
By symmetry $FGHI$ has four equal sides, so its perimeter is $4\cdot\frac{2\sqrt2}3=\frac{8\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{8\sqrt2}3$**

solutions.title: Projection
solutions.body:
Let $J$ be the projection of $F$ onto the plane $ABCD$. The distance from $J$ to the line $AB$, measured along $MP$'s direction, is $MF\cos\angle FMP=\frac12\cdot\left(-\frac13\right)=-\frac16$ (negative: $J$ lies outside the square, beyond $AB$). Hence the distance between the projections of $F$ and $H$ is $2(\frac16+\frac12)=\frac43$ and, since $F,H$ are at equal heights, $FH=\frac43$. $FGHI$ is a square with diagonal $\frac43$, so its perimeter is $4\cdot\frac{4/3}{\sqrt2}=\frac{8\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{8\sqrt2}3$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $1$, $P$ its centre and $M$ the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$. The cornered square is built by attaching to the square the pyramid $EABCD$ (apex $E$ above $P$, all faces equilateral triangles) and then attaching corner pyramids with apexes $F,G,H,I$ to the faces $EAB$, $EBC$, $ECD$, $EDA$ respectively (see the figure). Compute the volume of the cornered square.

solutions.title: Eight corner pyramids
solutions.body:
The pyramid $EABCD$ (height $\frac{\sqrt2}2$) is the union of four corner pyramids with base edge $1$ and four more corner pyramids (apexes $F,G,H,I$) are attached, so the cornered square consists of $8$ congruent corner pyramids with base an equilateral triangle of side $1$. Each has volume $\frac13\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot\frac1{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt2}{24}$ (height $DP=\frac1{\sqrt6}$ from problem 1). Total: $8\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{24}=\frac{\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt2}3$**

solutions.title: Twice the pyramid
solutions.body:
The cornered square is $EABCD$ together with four corner pyramids of the same total volume as the four corner pyramids that make up $EABCD$, so its volume is twice $\operatorname{vol}(EABCD)=2\cdot\frac13\cdot1\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2=\frac{\sqrt2}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt2}3$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. To *corner* a polyhedron means that the cornered faces do not overlap. The *base angle* of a cornered face is the angle at which the cornered face rises above an edge of the original face (for the cornered square this is $\angle FMP$ of problem 2(a)). Let $P$ be a right pentagonal prism whose $5$ lateral faces are congruent squares (its bases are regular pentagons of the same edge). Prove that it is possible to corner $P$; i.e., show that the cornered faces do not overlap. The proof may use calculator approximations.
answer: At every edge the dihedral angle of the prism plus the two base angles is less than $360^\circ$ (about $327^\circ$ at a square-square edge and $292^\circ$ at a square-pentagon edge).

solutions.title: Check each type of edge
solutions.body:
Cornered faces on the two sides of an edge fit together without overlapping at that edge provided the dihedral angle of the prism at the edge plus the base angles of the two cornered faces is less than $360^\circ$.

*Edges between two squares (like $AB$).* The dihedral angle of the prism is the interior angle of the pentagon, $108^\circ$. By problem 2(a) the base angle of a cornered square is $\arccos\left(-\frac13\right)=90^\circ+\arcsin\frac13\approx109.47^\circ$ (indeed $\arcsin\frac13<\arcsin\frac12=30^\circ$). Total: $108^\circ+2\cdot109.47^\circ\approx326.9^\circ<360^\circ$.

*Edges between a square and a pentagon (like $AC$).* The dihedral angle is $90^\circ$. The base angle of a cornered pentagon is the base angle of the pentagonal pyramid with equilateral faces of edge $1$ plus the base angle $\theta=\arccos\frac1{\sqrt3}\approx54.74^\circ$ of a corner pyramid. The pyramid has apothem $\frac{\tan54^\circ}2\approx0.688$ and height $\sqrt{\frac34-\frac{\tan^254^\circ}4}\approx0.526$, so its base angle is $\arctan\frac{0.526}{0.688}\approx37.4^\circ$, and the cornered pentagon's base angle is about $92.1^\circ$, less than the cornered square's $109.47^\circ$. Total at $AC$: $90^\circ+109.47^\circ+92.1^\circ\approx291.6^\circ<360^\circ$ (even the crude bound $90^\circ+2\cdot120^\circ=330^\circ<360^\circ$ suffices).

*Alternative for the belt of squares.* The ten base angles of the cornered squares round the pentagonal prism's belt sum to $10\cdot109.47^\circ=1094.7^\circ$; this must be less than the sum of the exterior angles $5(360^\circ-108^\circ)=1260^\circ$ of the pentagon, which it is.

Hence no overlap occurs at any edge, and the pentagonal prism can be cornered. ∎

reviewNote: The book's solution quotes about 91.113 degrees for the base angle of a cornered pentagon; recomputing gives about 92.1 degrees. The conclusion is unaffected (the bound used is 120 degrees).

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. The figure shows a squat polyhedron (its net, and the folded solid): a band of ten squares around its "equator" (so the band forms a right decagonal prism) capped above and below by regular pentagons, triangles and further squares. Prove that it is impossible to corner this polyhedron; that is, show that the cornered faces do overlap. The proof may use calculator approximations.
answer: At an edge $AB$ between two equatorial squares the dihedral angle is $144^\circ$ and the two cornered squares need $2\cdot109.47^\circ$, total $>360^\circ$.

solutions.title: An edge that cannot close up
solutions.body:
The equatorial band of squares forms a right decagonal prism. Let $AB$ be an edge joining two of these squares; the dihedral angle of the polyhedron at $AB$ is the interior angle of a regular decagon, $144^\circ$. If $P$ could be cornered, the cornered squares attached to the two squares adjacent to $AB$ would have to fit around $AB$, i.e. $144^\circ+2\cdot\arccos\left(-\frac13\right)\le360^\circ$.

But $\arccos\left(-\frac13\right)\approx109.47^\circ$. (Without a calculator: $\cos108^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt5-1}4\approx-0.309>-\frac13$, so $\arccos\left(-\frac13\right)>108^\circ$.) Hence the total exceeds $144^\circ+2\cdot108^\circ=360^\circ$, so the cornered squares overlap and $P$ cannot be cornered. ∎

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* The pattern in the figure (twelve regular pentagons and twenty regular hexagons) can be folded into a soccer-ball-like polyhedron called a buckyball. Compute the number of its edges.

solutions.title: Count the sides
solutions.body:
A buckyball has $12$ pentagonal and $20$ hexagonal faces. Each edge belongs to exactly $2$ faces, so $E=\frac{5\cdot12+6\cdot20}2=\frac{180}2=90$.

**Answer: 90**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* The pattern in the figure (twelve regular pentagons and twenty regular hexagons) can be folded into a soccer-ball-like polyhedron called a buckyball, with three faces meeting at each vertex. Compute the number of its vertices.

solutions.title: Count the corners
solutions.body:
Three faces meet at each vertex, so $V=\frac{5\cdot12+6\cdot20}3=\frac{180}3=60$. Check with Euler's formula: $V-E+F=60-90+32=2$.

**Answer: 60**

A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. A buckyball has $12$ regular pentagonal faces and $20$ regular hexagonal faces (all edges equal), $90$ edges and $60$ vertices. A *cornered buckyball* is obtained by replacing each face by the corresponding cornered polygon. Compute the number of faces of a cornered buckyball.

solutions.title: Faces of each cornered polygon
solutions.body:
A cornered pentagon has $5$ pyramid faces, each covered by $3$ faces of a corner pyramid: $15$ faces. A cornered hexagon has $6$ triangles each covered by $3$ faces: $18$ faces. Total: $15\cdot12+18\cdot20=180+360=540$.

**Answer: 540**

A *cornered buckyball* is obtained by replacing each face by the corresponding cornered polygon. Compute the number of edges of a cornered buckyball.

solutions.title: Additional edges
solutions.body:
A cornered pentagon has $5$ new edges (the pyramid's lateral edges) and $5\cdot3=15$ new edges from the corner pyramids, i.e. $20$ edges in addition to the pentagon's own boundary. A cornered hexagon has $6$ (centre to vertices) $+\,18=24$ additional edges. So $E=90+20\cdot12+24\cdot20=90+240+480=810$.

**Answer: 810**

A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A buckyball has $12$ regular pentagonal faces and $20$ regular hexagonal faces (all edges equal), $90$ edges and $60$ vertices. A *cornered buckyball* is obtained by replacing each face by the corresponding cornered polygon. Compute the number of vertices of a cornered buckyball.

solutions.title: Additional vertices
solutions.body:
A cornered pentagon has $1$ (apex of the pyramid) $+\,5$ (apexes of the corner pyramids) $=6$ additional vertices; a cornered hexagon has $1+6=7$. So $V=60+6\cdot12+7\cdot20=60+72+140=272$. Euler check: $V-E+F=272-810+540=2$.

**Answer: 272**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. A regular tetrahedron is a pyramid all of whose faces are equilateral triangles. Prove that a cornered regular tetrahedron is a cube.
answer: A cube $ABCDEFGH$ is the regular tetrahedron $ACFH$ with the four corner pyramids $BACF$, $DACH$, $EAFH$, $GCFH$ attached.

solutions.title: Inscribe the tetrahedron in a cube
solutions.body: Let $ABCDEFGH$ be a cube. Its four vertices $A,C,F,H$ (alternate vertices) form a regular tetrahedron, since all six face diagonals are equal. The remaining four vertices $B,D,E,G$ each have three mutually perpendicular equal edges to the vertices of one face of $ACFH$: $BACF$, $DACH$, $EAFH$, $GCFH$ are corner pyramids (three edges at $B$, e.g. $BA,BC,BF$, are mutually perpendicular and equal). So the cube is the regular tetrahedron $ACFH$ with a corner pyramid attached to each face, i.e. a cornered regular tetrahedron. Any regular tetrahedron is similar to $ACFH$, and a corner pyramid on a face is determined by the face, so every cornered regular tetrahedron is a cube. ∎

solutions.title: Angle chase
solutions.body: Start with a regular tetrahedron $ACFH$ and attach corner pyramids $BACF$, $DACH$ on faces sharing the edge $AC$ (and similar ones on the other faces). Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. Then $\angle DMH$ and $\angle BMF$ are base angles $\theta$ of corner pyramids, with $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$. So $\angle DMB=2\theta+\angle FMH$, where $\angle FMH$ is the base angle of the tetrahedron: $\cos\angle FMH=\frac13=-\cos2\theta$ and $\sin\angle FMH=\frac{2\sqrt2}3=\sin2\theta$, so $\angle FMH=180^\circ-2\theta$. Therefore $\angle DMB=180^\circ$: $B$ and $D$ lie on a line through $M$ and $ABCD$ is a flat square face. The same holds at every edge of the tetrahedron, so the cornered tetrahedron has six square faces: it is a cube. ∎

A regular octahedron has $8$ faces which are equilateral triangles with $4$ faces meeting at each of its $6$ vertices. Prove that a cornered octahedron has double the volume of the original octahedron.
answer: The octahedron is the union of $8$ corner pyramids with apex at its centre; cornering adds $8$ congruent corner pyramids.

solutions.title: Eight corner pyramids
solutions.body:
Let $ABCDEF$ be a regular octahedron with centre $G$ ($A,C$ opposite, $B,D$ opposite, $E,F$ opposite). The segments $GA,GB,GC,GD,GE,GF$ are equal and mutually perpendicular in pairs. So each of the eight tetrahedra $GABE$, $GBCE$, $GCDE$, $GDAE$, $GABF$, $GBCF$, $GCDF$, $GDAF$ has three mutually perpendicular equal edges at $G$ and an equilateral base face: each is a corner pyramid with apex $G$, and these eight congruent corner pyramids fill the octahedron.

Cornering the octahedron attaches one corner pyramid, congruent to these, on each of its $8$ faces. The volume added is $8$ corner pyramids, the same as the volume of the octahedron. Hence the cornered octahedron has twice the volume of the original. ∎

prompt: *(Power Question 1997: cornered polyhedra.)* A *corner pyramid with apex $D$* is a tetrahedron $DABC$ in which $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral and $\triangle DAB$, $\triangle DBC$, $\triangle DAC$ are isosceles right triangles with the right angle at $D$ (it is a corner cut from a cube). A *cornered polygon* is: (a) an equilateral triangle with a corner pyramid attached on it, completely covering it; (b) a regular hexagon divided into six equilateral triangles, each covered by a corner pyramid; (c) a square to which is first attached a pyramid whose base is congruent to the square and whose faces are equilateral triangles, each triangular face then being covered by a corner pyramid as in (a); (d) the same construction with a regular pentagon. A *cornered polyhedron* is a polyhedron whose faces have been replaced by the corresponding cornered polygons. Cover each face of a regular octahedron with a regular tetrahedron (attached on the face, outside) and then corner the resulting figure (attach a corner pyramid to every exposed triangular face). Prove that the cornered figure is a cube.
answer: Take the regular octahedron formed by the face centres of a cube; each corner octant of the cube is filled by a tetrahedron on one face and three corner pyramids on the tetrahedron's other faces.

solutions.title: Cube octants
solutions.body:
The centres of the faces of a cube of side $s$ are the vertices of a regular octahedron (edge $\frac s{\sqrt2}$). We show that covering its faces with regular tetrahedra and cornering gives back the cube.

Let $A$ be a vertex of the cube, $X,Y,Z$ the centres of the three faces at $A$, and $M,N,P$ the midpoints of the three cube edges at $A$. Then $AX=AY=AZ=XY=YZ=ZX=\frac{s}{\sqrt2}$, so $AXYZ$ is a regular tetrahedron attached to the octahedron's face $XYZ$. The faces $AXY$, $AXZ$, $AYZ$ are exposed. The tetrahedron $MAXY$ (with $M$ the midpoint of the edge shared by the two faces with centres $X,Y$) has $MA=MX=MY=\frac s2$ with $MA,MX,MY$ mutually perpendicular: a corner pyramid on the face $AXY$. Similarly $NAXZ$ and $PAYZ$ are corner pyramids. Together, $AXYZ$, $MAXY$, $NAXZ$, $PAYZ$ and the part of the octahedron inside this octant (the corner pyramid with apex the cube's centre on face $XYZ$) fill the sub-cube of side $\frac s2$ at $A$ (the $A$-octant), the tetrahedron $AXYZ$ and the four corner pyramids being the five pieces obtained by cutting alternate vertices from that sub-cube. The same happens at each of the $8$ vertices of the cube, so the whole figure is the cube. ∎

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* Let $P_1,P_2,P_3,\dots$ be a sequence of polyhedra where $P_1$ is a regular tetrahedron of side $1$. Create polyhedron $P_{n+1}$ from $P_n$ as follows: to each equilateral triangle face of $P_n$ attach a regular tetrahedron with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of that face (and one more vertex outside). Compute the number of faces of $P_n$.

solutions.title: Each face becomes six
solutions.body:
Attaching the tetrahedron on the middle triangle of a face leaves three corner triangles of that face and adds three new faces of the tetrahedron: each face is replaced by $6$ faces. With $4$ faces in $P_1$, $P_n$ has $4\cdot6^{n-1}$ faces.

**Answer: $4\cdot6^{n-1}$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* Let $P_1,P_2,P_3,\dots$ be a sequence of polyhedra where $P_1$ is a regular tetrahedron of side $1$. Create polyhedron $P_{n+1}$ from $P_n$ as follows: to each equilateral triangle face of $P_n$ attach a regular tetrahedron with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of that face (and one more vertex outside). Compute the surface area of $P_n$.

solutions.title: Face area times number of faces
solutions.body:
Each face of $P_n$ is an equilateral triangle of side $\frac1{2^{n-1}}$, of area $\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot\frac1{4^{n-1}}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4^n}$. The surface area is $4\cdot6^{n-1}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4^n}=\sqrt3\left(\frac64\right)^{n-1}=\sqrt3\left(\frac32\right)^{n-1}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3\left(\frac32\right)^{n-1}$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* Let $P_1,P_2,P_3,\dots$ be a sequence of polyhedra where $P_1$ is a regular tetrahedron of side $1$. Create polyhedron $P_{n+1}$ from $P_n$ as follows: to each equilateral triangle face of $P_n$ attach a regular tetrahedron with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of that face (and one more vertex outside). Find the limit, as $n$ goes to infinity, of the volume of $P_n$.

solutions.title: Geometric series
solutions.body:
$\operatorname{vol}(P_1)=\frac{\sqrt2}{12}=\frac1{6\sqrt2}$. Going from $P_n$ to $P_{n+1}$ we add $4\cdot6^{n-1}$ tetrahedra of side $\frac1{2^n}$, each of volume $\frac1{8^n}\cdot\frac1{6\sqrt2}$. So
$$\operatorname{vol}(P_{n+1})=\operatorname{vol}(P_n)+\frac{4\cdot6^{n-1}}{8^n}\cdot\frac1{6\sqrt2}=\operatorname{vol}(P_n)+\frac1{9\sqrt2}\left(\frac34\right)^n.$$
Summing, $\operatorname{vol}(P_{n+1})=\frac1{6\sqrt2}+\frac1{9\sqrt2}\sum_{k=1}^n\left(\frac34\right)^k\to\frac1{6\sqrt2}+\frac1{9\sqrt2}\cdot3=\frac1{6\sqrt2}+\frac1{3\sqrt2}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt2}4$.

**Answer: $\frac1{2\sqrt2}$**

prompt: *(Power Question 1997.)* Let $P_1,P_2,P_3,\dots$ be a sequence of polyhedra where $P_1$ is a regular tetrahedron of side $1$. Create polyhedron $P_{n+1}$ from $P_n$ as follows: to each equilateral triangle face of $P_n$ attach a regular tetrahedron with vertices at the midpoints of the sides of that face (and one more vertex outside). Prove that every $P_n$ fits inside a cube of side $\frac1{\sqrt2}$.
answer: $P_1$ is inscribed in the cube; every tetrahedron added at a later stage lies in a sub-cube, in the same position relative to it as $P_1$ is to the cube.

solutions.title: Self-similarity in a cube
solutions.body:
Place $P_1$ inside a cube $K$ of side $s=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ with its four vertices at four alternate vertices of $K$ (the face diagonals have length $s\sqrt2=1$). The midpoints of the edges of $P_1$ are the centres of the six faces of $K$.

Let $ABC$ be a face of $P_1$, $M,N,P$ the midpoints of its sides, and $D$ the vertex of $K$ adjacent to $A,B,C$ (the one not in $P_1$ on the side of $ABC$). The tetrahedron attached to $ABC$ at the first stage is $DMNP$: $D$ is a vertex of $K$ and $M,N,P$ are centres of the three faces of $K$ at $D$, so $DM=DN=DP=\frac s{\sqrt2}=\frac12=MN=NP=PM$ — a regular tetrahedron of edge $\frac12$, as required, and it lies in the sub-cube $K_D$ of side $\frac s2$ with a vertex at $D$, as four alternate vertices of $K_D$. That is exactly the position of $P_1$ in $K$, scaled by $\frac12$.

Likewise the corner tetrahedra of $P_1$ at $A,B,C,\dots$ lie in the sub-cubes at those vertices in the same position. So the eight sub-cubes of $K$ contain eight small tetrahedra, each in the same position as $P_1$ in $K$ (scaled by $\frac12$), together with the central octahedron of $P_1$. Every later attachment is made on a face of one of these small tetrahedra, so by the same argument (applied inside the sub-cube, then the sub-sub-cube, and so on) it lies in the corresponding smaller cube. Since no added tetrahedron ever leaves its cubelet, no $P_n$ leaves $K$. ∎
